title: Kula Disaster Recovery Update Meeting: December 19, 2023

issues.title: Extending property tax relief for wildfire-hit properties
Moving fire survivors off FEMA interim housing

recap.headline: Kula wildfire recovery update: debris nearly done, lead worries, insurance and housing
recap.in_60_seconds: County, State and federal agencies held their last weekly Kula wildfire recovery meeting of 2023, with presentations from MEMA, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the Department of Water Supply, the State Department of Health and FEMA. The Corps reported 20 Kula parcels cleared of debris. Water Supply said Upcountry restrictions will ease to stage one with watering one day a week. Four residents spoke about lead and ash exposure beyond burned lots, insurance living expenses running out, short-term rentals and taxes, and homes still standing in burned areas. The Mayor explained a property tax incentive for owners who rent to displaced families, and FEMA said it can help when insurance living expenses run out. Requests for wider lead testing, a review of the full burn area, and help for ash on unburned properties got no firm answer; the next meeting is expected January 9.

parts.title: Welcome and MEMA message
presented: Last weekly Kula meeting until January; meals were handed out to attendees.
MEMA thanked residents and said it will step back as the County moves into a recovery posture, while preparing for future emergencies.

next.what: MEMA steps back as recovery phase begins

parts.title: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers debris removal update
parts.presenter: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers colonel
presented: 20 Kula parcels have all debris removed; 11 of those have all paperwork complete.
Two crews are still working in Kula, including a crane job removing a structure from a gulch, expected to finish fairly quickly.
Each parcel gets a closeout package with a clean-property affidavit for the County, which the County uses for building permits, and a clearance report for FEMA.
The Corps asked Kula owners to share their experience with Lahaina residents, where the mission continues next.

next.what: Corps continues debris mission in Lahaina

parts.title: Department of Water Supply update
parts.presenter: Department of Water Supply deputy director
presented: Upcountry reservoirs are at about 90 percent or more; the water shortage will change to stage one.
Watering will be allowed one day a week, scheduled by area such as Pukalani, Makawao, Haʻikū and Kula.
Fire-affected homes do not need backflow devices unless they have a swimming pool, water tank or well.
Daily reservoir levels are now on the department website, except weekends.

next.what: Press release and map on the one-day-a-week watering schedule

parts.title: State Department of Health update
parts.presenter: State Department of Health deputy director for environmental health
presented: Last week's lead screening found four people with elevated levels, not one; they were asked to follow up with their doctors.
Two weeks of air sampling showed no asbestos and heavy metals below screening levels; a third week of results is being evaluated.
As of December 15 there are 25 PurpleAir sensors and six other monitors in Kula and Makawao; some may move to Lahaina as the Corps leaves Kula.

next.what: Third week of air sampling results posted on the DOH website

parts.title: FEMA assistance and housing update
presented: Almost $40 million in individual assistance provided so far; SBA has provided $282 million in loans and extended its deadline.
FEMA seeks owners of vacation rentals and other vacant units to lease to FEMA for at least a year, up to two years, for displaced families.
FEMA would act as landlord, pay rent at a reasonable rate, and cover damage and HOA fees.

next.what: Industry day for property owners at the Westin Maui Resort and Spa, 9 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.

parts.title: Questions on lead and ash exposure

raised.concern: A resident whose blood lead rose about tenfold after the fire asked for much wider lead testing in Kula, with flyers and questionnaires, possibly run by University of Hawaiʻi scientists, and noted the testing van was not there.
Toxic ash spread by high winds onto properties below the burned homes, and those owners get no debris help.
The burn area and property damage in Kula are undercounted; residents asked who reviews satellite imagery and for a projected map to discuss it, and several in the room said they wanted this.

answered.said: Restated the request as looking at the full burn extent and making sure properties are canvassed properly, then moved to the next question.

parts.title: Questions on insurance, housing and taxes

raised.concern: A fire survivor said the insurance commissioner was absent and asked why Hawaiʻi has not extended insurance living expenses as other states did, saying families cannot budget to rebuild without knowing lodging costs.
A realtor asked whether short-term rental permits are still being issued.
The same speaker asked to hold off new building while existing housing is used for displaced families, saying new housing draws people from out of state.
Concern that some owners may face higher property taxes under the rental incentive plan.
How households whose homes still stand but are unsafe to enter, with neighbors' homes gone, are helped when insurance living expenses run out.

answered.said: Apologized that the insurance commissioner could not attend and said they will get the commissioner there as soon as possible.
Said the County is not issuing more short-term rental permits.

Explained that the first 3,000 owners who rent units to displaced families get tax waivers and other non-owner-occupied, short-term rental and timeshare owners will be taxed only enough to cover the shortfall; signing up by January 31 gives 18 months of relief, March gives 12. The County is also re-evaluating relief for homes standing but unlivable.

Said FEMA caps rental assistance near long-term market rates to avoid driving up rents, negotiates short-term rental rates from past earnings, and that building already-planned affordable housing must continue alongside temporary capacity.

Said owners whose insurance living expenses run out while rebuilding can come back to FEMA for housing help if registered and working toward a plan; FEMA will look into what California did and contact the state insurance commissioner.
Said displaced owners should use insurance first; if still displaced, FEMA can discuss direct housing, but help ends once utilities return and the County deems the area safe.

next.what: Property tax relief sign-up for owners renting to displaced families: 18 months of relief
FEMA to review California's approach and contact the state insurance commissioner

parts.title: Announcements
presented: Handout with QR code for the MauiRecovers.org website.
No community meetings for the next two weeks.

parts.title: Mayor's closing remarks
presented: Thanked the state Department of Education for the meeting site.
Said all levels of government share the goal of getting residents home safely and quickly.
Said mental wellness, including worry about ash and lead, matters as much as housing, and urged neighbors to care for each other.

bills.name: Bill 131
bills.what: Property tax relief for owners who make units available as long-term housing for displaced fire survivors, with a later bill to set taxes covering the shortfall.

open_questions.question: Will the State expand blood lead testing across the Kula burn area and nearby homes?
Who reviews satellite imagery of the burn area, and will the full burn extent be shown and re-canvassed?
Will owners of unburned properties with ash and fire debris get cleanup help?
Will Hawaiʻi require insurers to extend additional living expense coverage as some other states did?
How much will property taxes rise for owners who do not join the rental program?

not_on_tracker.topic: Ash and fire debris on unburned Kula properties
not_on_tracker.why: Neighbors below burned homes say they live with toxic ash but get no cleanup help.

not_on_tracker.topic: Insurance living expenses running out before rebuilding
not_on_tracker.why: Fire survivors cannot budget to rebuild without knowing how long lodging will be covered.

not_on_tracker.topic: Property tax incentive for renting to displaced families
not_on_tracker.why: Owners of second homes and short-term rentals face either relief or higher taxes depending on whether they sign up.

moments.who: State Department of Health deputy director for environmental health
moments.quote: So far we've had two weeks of air sampling that showed that there was no asbestos in the air and heavy metals were lower than the screening levels.
moments.about: Early Department of Health air sampling in Kula after the fire found no asbestos, and heavy metals were below screening levels.

moments.who: A Kula resident living near burned homes
moments.quote: You need to do extensive, a lot of testing of people in the Kula area. I would farm this out. I would approach the University of Hawaii, get their research scientists to conduct the study for you.
moments.about: A Kula resident living below the burned properties called for a broad health study of ash exposure, saying only 14 people had been tested so far.

moments.who: A Maui realtor and property manager
moments.quote: And it's a great idea to get the tax advantages. I'm concerned that some of us may get hit with higher taxes.
moments.about: A local property manager worried that the tax breaks for fire housing could mean higher taxes for other owners.

moments.quote: You know, right after the fires, the week after the fires, we obviously waived all the property taxes for everyone here in Kula and everyone in Lahaina.
moments.about: The Mayor explained that property taxes were waived for burned properties in Kula and Lahaina right after the fires.

moments.quote: And so we're re-evaluating some of those that we might have denied. And now that we know more information, we can decide if... So I guess I'm going to say it this way, if you can live in your house but you choose not to, that's a different category than if you want to live in your house but you cannot.
moments.about: The county said it was re-evaluating denied tax relief for homes that were still standing but could not be lived in.

moments.quote: January 31st, if you sign up by then, you get 18 months of property tax relief.
moments.about: Owners who made units available to house fire survivors by January 31 would get 18 months of property tax relief, and 12 months if they signed up in March.
